Ethical Issues in Medicine and Research
Introduction to Bioethics
HTI5005
MP + MDS
Liang-Ting Lin

Why should we learn this subject, Ethical issues in Medicine and
Research?
To kick start this subject… one question

• As healthcare professionals, we will deal with life-and-death
situations as well as ethical dilemmas.
• It’s crucial to respect patients’ right and to safe-guard your own interests.
• This subject provides an overview of healthcare ethics.
• The principles and theories introduced in this subject underlie our
ethical thinking and decision making.
Backgrounds – a formal reason studying Ethics

• This subject introduce philosophical approaches including ethical
principles/theories and legal rules.
• When discussing real world ethical challenges in medicine, you may
come across “grey area”
So basically speaking, we deliver…
Quick Example – Moral or Ethical?
Now, here we go

Philosophy…

Ethical philosophy started with the ancient Greeks.
• The ancient virtues included:
1. Wisdom
2. Justice
3. Courage
4. Moderation
5. Piety
11
Ethics/Moral Philosophy – the Western viewpoint

• Ancient Greek physician
• The “Father” of western medicine
• Hippocratic medicine was notable for its strict professionalism,
discipline, and rigorous practice.
12
Hippocrates (460-370 BC)

Confucius (551 to 497 BC) 孔丘，字仲尼
• Central Dogma of Confucianism (儒家思想): 仁 Ren
• 子貢問仁。子曰：「何事於仁，必也聖乎！堯舜其猶病
諸！夫仁者，己欲立而立人，己欲達而達人。能近取譬，
可謂仁之方也。」
• 仲弓問仁。子曰：「出門如見大賓，使民如承大祭。己
所不欲，勿施於人。」
• 顏淵問仁。子曰：「克己復禮為仁，一日克己復禮，天
下歸仁焉。為仁由己，而由人乎哉？」
• Prone to Communitarianism, rather than
Liberalism – less individualism
13
Ethics/Moral Philosophy – the Chinese viewpoint

14
The Normative Ethics
First thing first – Ethics vs. Morals

• Bioethics is the interdisciplinary study of ethical issues arising in the life sciences,
health care, and health/science policy.
• Modern bioethics is widely held to have arisen in the late 1960s.
• Since then, it has helped transform the practice of medicine and inform policy-
making about accumulating issues concerning the life sciences, from public
health to the delivery of medical care.
Bioethics, Medical ethics and Healthcare ethics

• Respect for autonomy 自主原則
• Principle protecting one’s right to make his/her own decisions
• Beneficence 行善原則
• Principle of “doing good”
• Nonmaleficence 不傷害原則
• Principle of avoiding harm
• Justice 正義原則
• Principle describing the obligation to be fair in the distribution of
benefits and risk
22
Four Principles of Ethics (East or West?)
Tom Beauchamp and James Childress, 1994
It is important to note that no one value is weighted as greater than the other.
The lack of hierarchy means that different providers or systems may come to different ethical conclusions or decisions
when faced with a decision to be made.

• Respect for autonomy 自主原則
• Autonomy is Latin for "self-rule”
• Patient autonomy refers to the patient’s right to make decisions
for themselves according to their own system of morals and
beliefs.
• We have an obligation to respect the autonomy of other persons,
which is to respect the decisions made by other people concerning
their own lives.
• This is also called the principle of human dignity.
23
Four Principles of Ethics (1)

• Incompetence- patient is legally deemed unable to make rational
decision for themselves. Often due to permanent conditions such as
dementia. Assigned a surrogate by the court.
• Incapacity- patient is clinically determined to be unable to make
rational decision for themselves. May be due to transient conditions
such as lack of conciseness, delirium, psychosis, etc.
• Threat to self or others—usually in psychiatric settings.
24
When is autonomy compromised?

• Two appellants had been baptised as one of Jehovah’s Witnesses and
conscientiously rejects blood transfusions as an article of faith.
• Appellant E (16y 8m) was scheduled for appendectomy and declared
refusal of blood transfusion.
• Herself and her parents refused blood transfusion in a written format
• Plymouth Hospital filed a hearing seeking legal permission for blood
transfusion to avoid any intraoperative bleeding
• The right of blood transfusion for her was granted for the surgery
• What’s next?
26
Case Study – Blood Transfusion
Court order – Case E

• Two appellants had been baptised as one of Jehovah’s Witnesses and
conscientiously rejects blood transfusions as an article of faith.
• Appellant F (17y 5m) was hospitalized from a traffic accident and is
diagnosed with spleen laceration and internal bleeding, not instant
life-threatening.
• Appellant F refused blood transfusion.
28
Case Study – Blood Transfusion
Court Order – Case F

• By s. 8 Family Law Reform Act 1969, Parliament has provided that a person aged
16 and 17 has the right to consent to any recommended medical treatment, and
the House of Lords has held in Gillick that even individuals under 16 can make
their own decisions in certain circumstances.
• Risk is an inherent part of daily life and young persons are exposed to many
risks – riding bikes, dangerous sports, viruses – but the law does not intervene in
such matters.
• The starting point is a strong presumption in favour of a young person’s capacious
decision. The decision should be respected unless there are very strong reasons
for rejecting it.
OK, now we have some arguments

• Is age a matter of decision-making?
• When do you think you’re old enough to make decisions?
• What is the “best interest” in the two cases?
• Do you agree with the court order for E?
• Do you agree with the court order for F?
• If you were the doctor, what will you do?
• If you were the judge, what order will you follow to make decisions?
OK, in plain English

• Beneficence 行善原則
• Principle of “doing good”
• Beneficence is a value in which  the provider take actions or
recommends courses that are in the patients’ best interest
• Keep the individual patient in mind – beneficence is not the same
in all situations
• We have an obligation to bring about good in all our actions.
• When patient autonomy is compromised (e.g. incapacity),
beneficence must be the guiding ethic
32
Four Principles of Ethics (2)

• Nonmaleficence 不傷害原則
• We have an obligation not to harm others: "First, do no harm."
• Where harm cannot be avoided, we are obligated to minimize the harm we do.
• Don't increase the risk of harm to others.
• Combining beneficence and nonmaleficence: Each action must produce more
good than harm.
• The principle of double effect: Unintended medical consequences are acceptable if
the intended consequences are legitimate and the harm is proportionately smaller
than the benefit
1) Removing an organ or limb that is causing disease
2) Providing high-dose analgesics to a hospice patient even though it may
unintentionally shorten life
3) Controversial: Performing an unrequested abortion to save the mother’s life.
33
Four Principles of Ethics (3)

• Justice 正義原則
• It refers to respect for human rights and social justice.
• It describes the obligation to be fair in the distribution of benefits
and risk.
• In public life, we have an obligation to treat all people equally,
fairly, and impartially.
35
Four Principles of Ethics (4)

• Distributive justice is the proper allocation of resources in a manner that is fair
and just
• It is not necessarily equal allocation of resources
• Triage is a common example of distributive justice: The first person through the
doors of the emergency room is not necessarily attended to first (ankle sprain vs.
myocardial infarction)
36
Distributive justice

• Although the four principles appear straightforward and somewhat obvious, they
are frequently in conflict with one another.
• Ethical dilemmas arise when one principle directs a physician towards a certain
course of action, while another principle directs to a different one.
• When dealing with difficult scenarios, other frameworks of analysis are required.
37
Summary of Four Principles
Wait… Justice? What’s that?

A Theory of Justice – John Rawls
John Rawls (1921 – 2002)
“Justice is the first virtue of social institutions, as truth is of
systems of thought.” – A Theory of Justice: Definition
“My aim is to present a conception of justice which generalizes
and carries to a higher level of abstraction the familiar theory
of the social contract.” – A Theory of Justice: Justice as Fairness
“No one knows his place in society, his class position or social
status; nor does he know his fortune in the distribution of natural
assets and abilities.” – A Theory of Justice: Veil of Ignorance

1. “Each person is to have an equal right to the most extensive basic
liberty compatible with a similar liberty for others.”
2. “Social and economic inequalities are to be arranged so that they
are to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged.”
3. “A society is well-ordered when it is regulated by a public
conception of justice that everyone can reasonably accept.”
Rawls Theory – Justice

• Cake-cutting Parable (procedural justice):
• A group of people needs to divide a cake, and everyone naturally wants to get
the largest possible slice
• The person who cuts the cake must take the last slice
• Pure Procedural Justice: Because the cutter knows they will receive whatever
slice is left, their only rational strategy to maximize their share is to slice every
piece as equally as possible.
• A Microcosm of the Veil of Ignorance: In effect, the cutter operates without
knowing which specific slice they will ultimately possess, compelling them to
choose the most equitable distribution.
Wait…What are you talking about…

• The Scenario: When allocating limited medical resources, should
healthcare operate entirely as an unregulated market (capitalism, pay
more, get more), or should the state enforce a pooled system that
prioritizes the critically ill and economically disadvantaged?
• Behind the Veil of Ignorance: Before knowing your position in society,
you do not know whether you will be born with robust genetic health
or a debilitating chronic illness, nor can you guarantee you won't
suffer a catastrophic accident tomorrow.
• The Difference Principle: Socioeconomic inequalities are justifiable
only if they work to the maximum benefit of the least advantaged
members of society. In HK, higher earners and healthy contributors
subsidize (via Tax) the extensive medical costs of the severely ill and
impoverished, guaranteeing that the baseline standard of well-being
for the worst-off is preserved.
Healthcare System and Difference Principles

• Morals are our own principles.
• In most cases, when any one of us does something, we try to act
according to what society believes is right.
• Moreover, we listen closely to what our own believes about right or
wrong are telling us, even if they’re different from society’s views.
What are “morals”

• A dilemma is a situation where a person is
forced to choose between two or more
conflicting options, neither of which is
acceptable
What is a DILEMMA?

• Moral dilemmas are situations where persons, who are called moral
agents in ethics, are forced to choose between two or more
conflicting options, neither of which resolves the situation in a
morally acceptable manner.
• Moral dilemmas challenge our principles and decision-making.
• They often involve conflicting values and responsibilities.
• Analyzing moral dilemmas helps develop critical thinking skills.
Moral/Ethical Dilemmas
The Trolley Problem

Situation 1:
• There is a trolley coming down the tracks and ahead,
there are five people tied to the tracks and are unable
to move. The trolley will continue coming and will kill
the five people.
• There is nothing you can do to rescue the five people
EXCEPT that there is a lever. If you pull the lever, the
train will be directed to another track, which has ONE
person tied to it.
• You have two choices:
a) Do nothing, and the five people will die
b) Or pull the lever and save the five people, but that
one person will die.
The Trolley Problem

Situation 2:
• There is a trolley coming down the tracks and ahead,
there are five people tied to the tracks and are unable to
move. The trolley will continue coming and will kill the
five people.
• However, in this situation, you are standing on a bridge
above the track, and you can see the train coming. There
is a man standing next to you, who is so enormous and
heavy that if he places himself in front of the oncoming
train, it will hit and kill him, but the train will stop.
• You have two choices:
a) Do nothing and the five people will die.
b) Push the big guy down the bridge. He will be killed but will
stop the trolley and save the five people.
c) You can’t move big guy, and he’s pissed and throw you
down the track. Six people die.
The Trolley Problem

1.The person or the agent of a moral action is obliged to make a
decision about which course of action is best.
2.There must be different courses of action to choose from.
3.No matter what course of action is taken, some moral principles are
always compromised.
Three conditions present in moral dilemmas?
Second thing second – Ethics vs. Morals

• The word "ethics" is derived from the Greek word ethos (character)
• right and wrong; good and bad, and values in general
• Ethics can be defined as the framework to evaluate right versus wrong
decision
• A branch of philosophy formerly regarded by ancient Greeks as the “the
science of morals”
What is “ethics”?

• Ethics aims to figure out what the right thing is to do or what the
best course of action is.
• Understanding determinations and motivations based on conceptions of
right and wrong.
• No rigid guidelines or strict rules
• Relatively stable but can change over time as people's conception
change.
• It helps people decide how to behave and how to treat one
another and what values should prevail.
The purpose of Ethics

• Ethics can be defined as the framework to evaluate right versus
wrong decision.
• A system or code of conduct and morals advocated by a particular
individual or group.
• Laws related to healthcare
54
How to make a (right or wrong) decision?

Healthcare ethics provides basic principles and theories in solving
specific controversial issues:
1) Breach of confidentiality
2) Informed consent and patient competence
3) Rationing of scarce medical resources
4) End-of-life care
56
Those basic principles of Healthcare Ethics

• Ethics ≠Moral values (feelings)
• Ethics ≠Religious believes
• Healthcare ethics ≠ Social standards
• Ethics ≠ Law
57
Healthcare Ethics

59
The paradigm of physician-patient relationship

Google can’t treat you
• Patients deliberately want to know more
about their symptoms and options
• Despite proper discussion, some
patients question or confront physicians
for their decisions
• How about your professions?
• Medical Physics?
• Medical Data Science?

• The patients, their families and the general public have increased
requirements and expectations on healthcare professionals.
• As healthcare professionals, in addition to profession-related knowledge
and skills, legal and ethical issues become core curricula
• As healthcare professionals, we should know how to respect patients’ right
and how to safeguard your own interests.
62
Healthcare ethics in contemporary medicine

Hippocratic Oath

I swear by Apollo Healer, by Asclepius, by Hygieia, by Panacea, and by all the gods and goddesses, making them
my witnesses, that I will carry out, according to my ability and judgment, this oath and this indenture.
To hold my teacher in this art equal to my own parents; to make him partner in my livelihood; when he is in
need of money to share mine with him; to consider his family as my own brothers, and to teach them this art, if
they want to learn it, without fee or indenture; to impart precept, oral instruction, and all other instruction to
my own sons, the sons of my teacher, and to indentured pupils who have taken the Healer's oath, but to
nobody else.
I will use those dietary regimens which will benefit my patients according to my greatest ability and judgment,
and I will do no harm or injustice to them. Neither will I administer a poison to anybody when asked to do so,
nor will I suggest such a course. Similarly I will not give to a woman a pessary to cause abortion. But I will keep
pure and holy both my life and my art. I will not use the knife, not even, verily, on sufferers from stone, but I will
give place to such as are craftsmen therein.
Into whatsoever houses I enter, I will enter to help the sick, and I will abstain from all intentional wrong-doing
and harm, especially from abusing the bodies of man or woman, bond or free. And whatsoever I shall see or
hear in the course of my profession, as well as outside my profession in my intercourse with men, if it be what
should not be published abroad, I will never divulge, holding such things to be holy secrets.
Now if I carry out this oath, and break it not, may I gain for ever reputation among all men for my life and for
my art; but if I break it and forswear myself, may the opposite befall me.
Hippocratic Oath (Translated to English)

“Do you believe I had to transfer a 200-kg guy from bed to CT table and transfer

Do you think it is proper to post this message in this way?

Case 1 – Social Media Post

• Privacy setting on your account does not guarantee that some relevant people
will not see your post.
• Before posting, ask if the information you are sharing could possibly reveal the
identity of the patient.
Case 1 – Social Media Post

• You are preparing for a presentation poster for a local conference.
• You included photos of one patient to show varying stages of clinical
interventions in the poster.
• What factors do you need to consider?
Case 2 – Use of Pictures/Medical Records

• Photos can provide information that links to identification of patients
• The conference attendees are not in this patient’ circle or care, so
they should not be receiving this information about the patient.
• Consider if the patient has given you consent to share the photo.
• The medical professionals are accountable for obtaining consent.
Case 2 – Use of Pictures/Medical Records

1. What is “Privacy”?
2. What is “Confidentiality”?
28
Something to clarify

“Privacy” is the ability of an individual or group to seclude themselves, or
information about themselves, and thereby express themselves selectively.
It also refers to a person’s desire to control the access of others to themselves.
Control or Limit Access
Control or Limit Information
Example: Persons may not want to be seen entering a place that might
stigmatize them, such as a pregnancy counseling center that is clearly
identified as such by signs on the front of the building.
29
Privacy (Nature)

• Cardi B was pregnant at the time but had not publicly disclosed it.
• The medical office (Ellis, the Plaintiff) was reportedly closed to other
patients for her privacy.
• Cardi B claimed Ellis followed her, said her name aloud, and possibly
recorded her.
• Cardi B admitted a verbal confrontation, denied any physical assault.
• Ellis later filed a civil case against Cardi B for assault, battery, and
consequential job loss.
• Cardi B was found NOT liable to the accusations.
Cardi B Case

“Confidentiality” involves a set of rules, or a promise usually executed through
confidentiality agreements that limits access or places restrictions on certain types
of information.
It also refers to certain agreements with anyone involved, about how the
identifiable private information will be handled, managed, and disseminated.
Protect Information
Disclose only in accordance with Permission, Rules or Laws
Confidentiality (Law)

In the field of healthcare,
• Healthcare professionals have an ethical duty to keep patient
information confidential.
• Medical records can only be shared with the patient’s permission.
• The confidentiality can only be breached in a few exceptions.
Confidentiality & Medical records

1)
It benefits patient by providing a secure environment
Patients often must share private, intimate and potentially embarrassing
personal details.
2)
It expresses respect for patients’ autonomy
People have a right to choose who will have access to information about them.
3)
It supports public trust confidence and trust in healthcare services more
generally.
Three Reasons for Confidentiality:
Privacy & Confidentiality

Personal data means any data "relating directly or indirectly to a living individual,
from which it is possible and practical to ascertain the identity of the individual
from the said data, in a form in which access to or processing of the data is
practicable”

1)
Name

Codes and Guidelines for Research Ethics

1.
Voluntary Consent: Participants must give informed and voluntary consent.
2.
Fruitful Results: Experiments should aim to produce beneficial results for society.
3.
Prior Research: Experiments must be based on prior knowledge or animal tests
4.
Avoid Unnecessary Harm: Avoid unnecessary physical and mental suffering.
5.
No Risk of Death: Experiments should not be conducted if there’s a risk of death or
severe injury, unless the researchers themselves participate.
6.
Proportional Risk: Risk should not exceed the potential humanitarian benefits.
7.
Adequate Preparation: Proper precautions and facilities must be in place to
minimize risk.
8.
Qualified Personnel: Only qualified individuals should conduct the experiments.
9.
Right to Withdraw: Participants can end their involvement at any time.
10. Stop if Dangerous: The experiment must be terminated if it risks causing harm.
Ten Points of the Nuremberg Code

• Respect for Persons:
• Individuals are autonomous and must be treated with dignity.
• Additional protections for those with limited autonomy, e.g., children, prisoners
• Beneficence:
• Maximize benefits while minimizing potential harm.
• Assess risks and benefits to ensure adherence to ethical research practices.
• Justice:
• Fair distribution of the benefits and burdens of research.
• Avoid exploiting vulnerable populations for research purposes
